common_name: Ellen Felton Dark Collard (North Carolina Family Heirloom Collard)
scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'Ellen Felton Dark'

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant for a fall crop, or sow in early spring; this variety tolerates cold down to about 20F, and light frost sweetens the leaves further.

directions: This slightly-heading collard traces to at least 1935 in Beaufort County, North Carolina, where a family seed saver grew and passed it down before it was shared with a USDA heirloom-collecting effort and later added to the Seed Savers Exchange catalog. The elliptic, wavy-to-toothed green leaves form a loosely gathered rather than open habit, distinguishing it from fully open Southern collards like Georgia Southern. Cooked leaves carry a notably sweet, faintly fruity flavor compared to more assertive collard types, and the plant handles hard cold well into the low 20s Fahrenheit.

common_name: Georgia Blue Stem Collard (Pre-1900 Southern Heirloom Collard)
scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'Georgia Blue Stem'

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting, or direct sow in late summer for a fall-through-winter Gulf South crop; large plants need room to spread.

directions: Documented under the names Blue Stem and Georgia Blue Stem in American seed literature predating 1900, this large heirloom was preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange member network before returning to wider circulation. Its obovate leaves are blue-green with prominent white midribs and a rounded, toothed margin, carried on a big, open plant with narrow petioles. It is prized among older Southern collard types for a notably sweet, juicy eating quality once cooked, distinct from the coarser bite of some other heirloom strains.

common_name: White Mountain Cabbage Collard (South Carolina Heading Heirloom)

planting.note: Sow in spring for a loose cabbage-like head by fall, following the traditional South Carolina cultivation timing for this family line.

directions: This South Carolina family heirloom was donated to Seed Savers Exchange along with a family memory of the leaves being used for homemade sauerkraut. Unlike open-leaf collards, White Mountain is compact with short stems, and when spring-sown it draws its yellow-green-blue leaves into a fairly tight cabbage-like head by fall rather than staying loose and upright. It represents the cabbage-collard branch of Southern collard breeding, alongside Yellow Cabbage Collard and Whaley's Favorite, where growers selected for a heading habit combined with collard-style leaf texture.

common_name: Whaley's Favorite Cabbage Collard (South Carolina Family Heirloom)

planting.note: Sow for a fall harvest; leaves sweeten and become more tender after light frost, and the plant can also be timed for spring crops in cooler zones.

directions: Kept for generations by a South Carolina family as a home-garden seed-saving tradition, this variety is part of the same cabbage-collard lineage as White Mountain and Yellow Cabbage Collard. Its broad, smooth, light-to-medium green leaves have slightly crinkled edges and gather into a loose, rounded, cabbage-like head rather than growing fully open like a typical collard. The texture is markedly more tender than standard collards, and the flavor is milder and sweeter, especially after a frost, which suits it to quick sautes as well as the long, slow-simmered pots traditional to Southern cooking.

common_name: Old Fashioned Ragged Edge Mustard (Hen Pecked Heirloom Mustard Green)

planting.note: Direct sow for a quick spring crop or, in the Gulf South, from late summer into fall for a winter harvest of greens.

directions: Also sold under the folk names Hen Pecked Mustard and Ragged Edged Mustard, this black-seeded, open-pollinated type is an old standby of Southern home gardens grown both for salad and cooking greens and for its own seed. The long, narrow leaves are deeply cut and ruffled along the margin, giving the variety its ragged edge name and setting it apart from the broader, less-dissected leaves of Southern Giant Curled or Florida Broadleaf. Flavor is notably sharp and aromatic, with a horseradish-like bite that mellows somewhat when cooked, and the short days-to-maturity make it a reliable fast crop for both spring and fall sowings.

common_name: Feaster Family Heirloom Mustard (Florida Family Mustard Green)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer through fall; a fast, mild mustard suited to the classic Southern greens rotation alongside turnip and collard greens.

directions: This family heirloom was grown and saved by generations of a family in rural Marion County, Florida, with stewardship reportedly reaching back to the Civil War era, before being shared with Seed Savers Exchange. The plant produces smooth green leaves that cook up milder and slightly sweeter than many Southern mustards, making it a gentler entry point for gardeners who find sharper types like Southern Giant Curled too pungent. Its fast maturity and mild flavor place it well alongside collard and turnip greens in a traditional fall Gulf Coast greens patch.
